en: Over a quarter of games after …d5, and the course had no reply.
We deliberately transpose into an open game: with the knight already on c6, it's an ordinary Italian or Ruy Lopez — familiar ground.
The Two Knights. Know this: the reply is …d5, and definitely NOT …Nxd5 afterwards.
The right defence. Recapturing on d5 loses to Nxf7 — the trap every 4.Ng5 player is hoping for.
We recapture with the queen: the c6 knight already guards her, so Nc3 gains no tempo as it would in the Scandinavian.
The quiet elder sister of the King's Indian: …d6 and …e5 WITHOUT the fianchetto, solid manoeuvring play with no weaknesses. Easy to grasp, hard to break.

One game in six. The Old Indian plays …d6 and …e5; against the London, …d5 is cleaner — the f4 bishop has no target left.
The Old Indian: …d6 to support …e5, no fianchetto — solid and easy to play.
The central break: challenging d4 at once.
The exchange leads to a queenless, sound endgame, perfectly holdable for Black.
The pin: trade the bishop for the f3-knight to make …e5 stronger.
The pin is still available: we've slipped from an Old Indian into a Nimzo by transposition, which is a good trade.
The deepest opening in the 1.e4 repertoire: the b5 bishop puts lasting pressure on c6 and e5. Patient positional pressure, rich in plans and systems.
Open the centre at once with 3.d4: clear play, active pieces, little heavy theory. Ideal for seizing the initiative without memorising tons of lines.
An aggressive cousin of the Italian: 2.Nc3 prepares f4. Rarely played, so dangerous at club level — and full of traps, right up to the Frankenstein-Dracula.
A venomous antique: 3.c3 prepares d4 to build a big centre. Rare, so disorienting; the two sound replies (…Nf6 and …d5) both require precision.
The most prestigious Sicilian: …a6 first, to prepare …e5 or …e6 with maximum flexibility. Demanding theory, huge reward.
The g7 bishop breathes fire down the long diagonal. Opposite-side castling and pawn races: the most explosive Sicilian.
The Classical Sicilian: both knights develop naturally (…Nc6, …Nf6) without the Najdorf (…a6) or Dragon (…g6) commitment. The main line is the Richter-Rauzer Attack (6.Bg5).
The great modern gamble: …e5 concedes the d5 hole but gives Black's pieces wild activity. Heavy theory, but very clear dynamic plans.
A flexible Sicilian: …e6 and …Nc6 without committing. Black decides late between …Qb6, …Bb4, …a6 and …d6 depending on White.
The chameleon Sicilian: …a6 first, keeping every structure available (Hedgehog, Scheveningen, …Bc5). Little forced theory, lots of understanding.
The small centre …e6/…d6: an elastic, weakness-free structure ready to uncoil with …d5 or …e5 at the right moment. The basis of many Sicilians.
With 1…d5 Black strikes the centre at once and dictates the plan: recapture with the queen, or counterattack with …Nf6. Sound, logical and easy to play.
Hypermodern: let White build a big centre… then harass it with the g7 bishop, …e5 and …c5. Flexible and tricky.
The defence of solidity: instead of defending e5, Black counterattacks e4 by symmetry. A famously tough equaliser — the bane of attacking players.
A hypermodern surprise weapon: 1…b6 and the b7 bishop press e4 along the long diagonal. Out of theory from move one, at the cost of a little space.
The classical opening par excellence: the Queen's Gambit puts lasting pressure on the centre. Black declines with …e6, solid but a touch passive.
Black grabs c4 — but can't hold the pawn. White regains the centre with e3/e4 and enjoys easy, free development.
The defence of activity: …c5 at once, accepting an isolated queen's pawn in exchange for free pieces and a crystal-clear plan. The most dynamic answer to the Queen's Gambit.
The Slav (…c6) keeps the c8 bishop free — its big edge over the QGD. This repertoire shows how White handles it, both pure Slav and Semi-Slav.
With 2.Bg5 you dodge heavy theory: the bishop pins f6 and imposes original play. Little to memorise, plenty of concrete plans.
A system opening, cousin of the Trompowsky: Nc3 + Bg5, pin f6 and aim for the e4 push. Little theory, concrete play and direct attacking ideas.
A quiet attacking system: Bg5 pins f6, then e3, Nbd2, c3, Bd3 and a kingside attack. Little theory, clear plans against almost everything.
The hypermodern opening par excellence: 1.Nf3 then c4 and a g2 fianchetto. Don't occupy the centre — undermine it from afar. Flexible, positional, little forced theory.
Solid and quiet: Black supports e5 with …d6 instead of …Nc6. Little space, but a weakness-free position with clear plans (…c6, …Be7, …0-0).
A surprise gambit in the Petrov: give back a pawn for wild development and deadly traps on f2 and e4. Dubious at heart, lethal in blitz.

Nearly a third of games, and the course started from 2.d4. White develops without committing — the most awkward treatment for us.
One game in five: White shuts the b7 bishop's diagonal. It must be reopened at once, or the piece is useless.
The pin is our main resource: without it White's centre becomes too comfortable and the b7 bishop bites on granite.
The undermining move: we hit the d5 pawn at its base. After the trade the b7 bishop regains the long diagonal and the game levels out.

Symmetry: Black meets the attack on e5 by attacking e4.
Careful: recapturing with …Nxe4 at once is a mistake. First …d6!
White opens the centre instead of taking e5. …Nxe4 is correct.
A third of games, and the course started from 3.Nxe5. White declines the Petrov debate and offers the Four Knights.
Nearly one game in five. Not dangerous, but you must know that …Nxe4 is perfectly playable here.
Kick the knight BEFORE taking on e4: move order is crucial.
The wrong order: recapturing without kicking the knight first. A classic trap looms.
Instead of d4, White offers a knight trade for a slight space edge.
The typical Petrov position: symmetrical, sound, famous for equality.
The deadly pin: after 4…Nf6?? 5.Nc6+! wins the queen. The ONLY move is 4…Qe7.
Oppose queens and prepare the …d6 fork: White cannot keep the loot.
We accept: symmetry holds no fear, and a Petrov player is looking for exactly this — sound, balanced positions.
Recapture towards the centre: the doubled pawns open the d-file and free the c8 bishop. The bishop pair more than compensates.
We take. Unlike the 3.Nxe5 line, no queen fork looms: the e4 knight will be held by the coming …d5.
The freeing move: we hit the c4 bishop and regain the pawn with a completely sound position.

Philidor — main line
vs 3.Nc3
Without 2.Nf3, the e5 pawn is not attacked: playing …d6 at once would be passive for no reason. One White player in nine, and the course had nothing.
The most common move against the Philidor — over four games in ten — and the course started from 3.d4. White eyes f7 before opening the centre.
White develops without pushing d4: one player in ten, and the course only planned for d4 and Bc4. Without d4, our position is not cramped at all.
Trade in the centre for simple, solid play, free of space worries.
Seven White players in ten take here, and the course had no answer. Careful: recapturing on d6 with the pawn loses precious time.
White restrains …b5; Black manoeuvres calmly behind the small centre.
Sober and correct: develop without offering a target. …Be6 would invite Bxe6 and a doubled pawn for nothing.
One White player in five castles at once instead of pushing d4, and the course only saw d4. The time they give us, we are going to use.
Quiet development, one White player in six. Same answer as above, and for the same reason.
The typical modern Philidor position: cramped but without weaknesses. The plan is …Re8, …Bf8 and …c6.
THE move to know: don't recapture on e5 — take on e4 instead. That's the resource the whole line rests on.
More than one White player in two takes on d6 rather than playing Qd5, and the course only planned for Qd5. It is the quiet line, and it must be known.
We hit e4 since we have time for it. The Philidor is a defence of necessity, not of principle: when the necessity is gone, we play something better.
We recapture with the BISHOP, not the queen: the queen on d6 would invite tempo moves, the bishop is simply well placed there.
The move that changes everything: since d4 is no longer playable on good terms, we take space instead of suffering it. The Philidor becomes a reversed Sicilian.
That move again: as soon as White gives up on d4, the d4 square becomes OUR business. It is the thread running through this whole chapter.
White goes for the bishop pair. Letting them take on e6 is no disaster: our e6 pawn will hold d5 and f5, and the position is closed.

The Pirc: the bishop goes to g7 and targets the centre from afar.
The most natural and safest development.
The Austrian Attack, the most ambitious: a huge centre with f5 in the air.
The 150 Attack: Qd2 and Bh6 to trade the strong g7 bishop, then h4-h5.
The Byrne: the bishop pins f6 at once, with Qd2 and 0-0-0 in mind.
White restrains the …b5 break before continuing.
The thematic central break: Black finally claims the centre.
The direct counter: hitting d4 before even castling.
Black counters at the right moment with …c5 or …e5.
Strike the d4 base; White's big centre becomes a target.
The queen regains c5 while hitting e5/c3: Black equalises the space.
White trades the dragon bishop; Black stays solid and hits back on the queenside.
Since they aren't pressing, we contest the centre AT ONCE — the Pirc is only worth playing if White's centre eventually gives.

Ponziani — 3.c3
Without …Nc6 there is no Ponziani: c3 serves no purpose if no knight is guarding e5. One player in six, and the course only planned for …Nc6.
The Petrov also sidesteps the Ponziani. One player in ten, and the course had nothing.
The Ponziani move: c3 supports d4, aiming for an imposing e4+d4 centre.
The active reply: hit e4 while White's b1-knight isn't out yet.
The central reply: hit e4 at once to defuse the d4 plan.
Over a quarter of games, and the course started from …Nf6 or …d5. The bishop on c5 opposes d4 — but c3 prepared precisely that.
One Black player in eight simply props up e5, and the course only planned for …Nf6, …d5 and …Bc5. It is passive, and it lets us build the whole centre.
Seven Black players in ten take here. The course went elsewhere, leaving the student alone in the most played line.
We push anyway. That's the Ponziani's whole point: building the centre with a prepared tempo.
More than four Black players in ten retreat rather than pin with …Bb4+, and the course only knew that pin. On b6 the bishop watches the centre without touching it.
Push rather than recapture: the f6 knight must run, and we gain the tempo that pays for the pawn.
The knight flees to g4 rather than d5 — nearly one Black player in four, and the course only planned for …Nd5. It is a mistake: the knight has no way back.
We change plan without hesitation: against a passive defence, the immediate break beats slow preparation.
The forced move, and the trap to know: …Nxe4 at once loses the queen to Qe2.
We close at the exact moment when the c6 knight has no good square: it must go to e7 and get in the f8 bishop's way. That is the whole point of c3.
We pin before they develop. Black has no good developing move left: every piece that comes out leaves a weakness behind it.
Forced, and fatal: we take on h6 and their kingside is wrecked before they have even castled. The concrete punishment of …Ng4.

The Slav: Black supports d5 with a pawn without shutting in the bishop. It too has its own course.
Black develops before committing. One player in seven, and the course only saw …dxc4, …e6 and …c6.

The ambitious version: White builds a big e4+d4 centre at once.
Black wants to hold c4 with …b5. It's an illusion: the pawn falls.
Nearly one Black player in five, and the course only planned for …Nf6 and …a6. They prepare …c5 while freeing the bishop.
We stop …b5 before it happens. Without that expansion, Black's c8 bishop stays the problem it has always been in the Accepted.
One Black player in four opens the way for the f8 bishop instead of hitting the centre with …e5. The course only saw …e5.
The attempt to keep the pawn. One Black player in five tries it, and the refutation must be known rather than improvised at the board.
Trade on e6 to hit b7 and e6 with the queen — a pawn usually returns.
The undermining blow: a4 hits the b5-c4 chain at its base.
The natural move. If …Bb4, that's the Ragozin; if …Nf6, the classical Declined position.
More than one Black player in two makes this natural developing move, and the course only planned for the pin …Bb4. It was this repertoire's biggest gap.
And we're back to OUR subject, a tempo up: a Slav that takes on c4 becomes a delayed Queen's Gambit Accepted.
The classical Queen's Gambit Declined pin: the f6 knight guards d5 and e4, and while it is pinned, Black's centre stands on one leg.
Black goes for trades to breathe. We let them: the h4 bishop goes for the e7 bishop, and we keep the better structure.
We hit the chain at its base: Black cannot hold everything, and every move they spend defending that pawn gives us one in the centre.
Modest and solid: we will recapture on c4 with the bishop, having never weakened the centre to get there.
